hook.line: This week everyone wants Tomás somewhere: salsa with Mariana, football with don Hernando, a party in Medellín. Plans come with conditions, and Spanish hangs every one of them on a tiny word: *si*, if.
hook.es: Si llueve, no vamos al partido.
hook.en: If it rains, we're not going to the match.

examples.en: If you want, we'll go to the cinema. (to a friend)

examples.es: Si llueve mañana, nos quedamos en el café.
examples.en: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay at the café.

examples.es: Si tienes tiempo esta tarde, ven al café.
examples.en: If you have time this afternoon, come to the café. (to a friend)
If you don't understand, ask. (to a friend)
If you go, I'll go. (to a friend)

examples.es: No vamos al partido si llueve.
examples.en: We're not going to the match if it rains.

examples.es: Si viene don Hernando, le hago un tinto.
examples.en: If don Hernando comes, I'll make him a coffee.

rule:
*Si* plus the plain present sets up the condition: *si quieres*, *si llueve*, *si tienes tiempo*.

The other half can be:
the present: *Si llueve, nos quedamos.*
*ir a*: *Si llueve, vamos a ver una película.*
an instruction: *Si tienes tiempo, ven.*

English says if it rains, we'll stay. Spanish usually drops the will and just says we stay: *nos quedamos*. That's normal, not lazy.

The *si* half can go first (with a comma) or second (no comma): *No vamos si llueve.*

One spelling trap: *si* with no accent is if. *Sí* with an accent is yes. They sound the same.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a real or open conditional: *si* plus the present indicative, for something that might really happen.

options: If we want, you'll go.
If you want, we'll go.
Yes, let's go.
If we go.
It's raining, so we're not going out.
If it rains, we're not going out.
If it doesn't rain, we're going out.

options: If I'm hungry, there are arepas in the kitchen.
If you're hungry, there are arepas in the kitchen.
If you go, I'll go.
If I go, you'll go.
If I call you, you'll come.
If you call me, I'll come.
If it's sunny, we'll go out.
It's sunny, so we're going out.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *si* or *sí* and type the whole sentence: ___ quieres, vamos al cine. (If you want, we'll go to the cinema.)
yourTurn.why: If is *si*, with no accent. *Sí* with an accent is yes.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *llueve* or *llover* and type the whole sentence: Si ___, nos quedamos en casa. (If it rains, we'll stay at home.)
yourTurn.answer: Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa.
accept: Nos quedamos en casa si llueve.
yourTurn.why: *Si* needs a real present form after it, like *llueve*, not the dictionary form.

yourTurn.prompt: Say to a friend: If you want, we'll go dancing on Friday.
yourTurn.answer: Si quieres, vamos a bailar el viernes.
accept: Vamos a bailar el viernes si quieres.
Si quieres, el viernes vamos a bailar.
yourTurn.why: *Si quieres* sets the condition, and the plan stays in the present: *vamos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say to a friend: If you have time this afternoon, come to the café.
yourTurn.answer: Si tienes tiempo esta tarde, ven al café.
accept: Ven al café si tienes tiempo esta tarde.
yourTurn.why: Condition in the present, then a plain instruction: *ven*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: If it rains, we're not going to the match.
yourTurn.answer: Si llueve, no vamos al partido.
accept: No vamos al partido si llueve.
yourTurn.why: English adds a going to or a will; Spanish is happy with the plain present: *no vamos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Put the *si* half second: *Si llueve, no salimos.*
yourTurn.why: Either order works. When *si* comes second, you don't need the comma.

yourTurn.prompt: Make the condition negative: *Si puedes ir, llama a Mariana.* (If you can't go...)
yourTurn.answer: Si no puedes ir, llama a Mariana.
accept: Llama a Mariana si no puedes ir.
yourTurn.why: *No* goes right before the verb, inside the *si* half: *si no puedes*.

pitfalls.why: Close. If has no accent: *si*. With an accent, *sí* means yes.

pitfalls.wrong: Si tendrás tiempo, ven al café.
pitfalls.right: Si tienes tiempo, ven al café.
pitfalls.why: English says if you have, not if you will have. Spanish is the same: the *si* half stays in the present.

pitfalls.wrong: Si llover, nos quedamos en casa.
pitfalls.right: Si llueve, nos quedamos en casa.
pitfalls.why: *Si* needs a real verb with a person in it, like *llueve* or *quieres*, not the dictionary form.

personal: Plan your weekend both ways: one sentence with *Si hace sol,* and one with *Si llueve,*.
